The final answer 1/(2t(t−1)) looks correct. I checked the argument but did not verify every step of the construction, and I did not check the even-q case, which the solution only gestures at.

**Upper bound.** If u, v lie on the same side A of a copy of K_{t,t} with other side B, then B ⊆ N(u)∩N(v). Since K_{2,t+1}-freeness gives |N(u)∩N(v)| ≤ t = |B|, we get B = N(u)∩N(v). The same holds for pairs on the B side. So every pair of vertices is a same-side pair of at most one copy. Each copy has 2·C(t,2) = t(t−1) same-side pairs, so the count is at most C(n,2)/(t(t−1)) ≈ n²/(2t(t−1)).

**Consistency check.** Near-tightness would need almost every pair to have exactly t common neighbours, which forces degree d ≈ √(tn). At a vertex u, the sets B must be t-subsets of N(u) that pairwise share at most one element. That allows about C(d,2)/C(t,2) ≈ d²/(t(t−1)) = n/(t−1) copies. This is exactly the number needed to cover all n pairs at u, so there is no hidden contradiction.

**Construction.** On q^{2e−1} vertices with q = t, the proposed graph has degree q^e = √(qn), matching the required degree. The common-neighbour count is exactly q for pairs with x ≠ y, via an affine condition modulo ker π = F_qθ. The vertices adjacent to all of a common neighbourhood B form a set of size q, so they complete a K_{q,q}. This covers almost all pairs, so the lower bound matches the upper bound asymptotically.

The limit is therefore 1/(2t(t−1)).

VERDICT: ACCEPT
